title: Managed Instability: Why the Wars Against Iran and Ukraine Can Go On and On and On…
gist: Alex Kolbin argues the Ukraine and Iran wars have both evolved past their original goal of quick victory into a self-sustaining condition he calls 'managed instability,' where key actors on all sides find continued conflict more advantageous than settlement, and the two wars are now materially entangled via Russia-Iran-Ukraine-Gulf technology and support flows, making resolution of either harder without resolving both.

insights.claim: Both the Russo-Ukrainian war and the 2026 Iran war began with a stronger power expecting overwhelming military force to produce a quick political capitulation, and in both cases that expectation failed, pushing the conflict into an open-ended contest over leverage rather than resolution.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: Investors pricing either war as heading toward a near-term settlement (and de-escalation of sanctions/shipping risk) should instead price a multi-year structural stalemate.
insights.locator: opening paragraphs

insights.claim: Kolbin defines 'managed instability' as the point where bargaining through violence stops being a path toward settlement and becomes the preferred operating condition of a war for enough key actors to block a deal, even if not all sides benefit from continued fighting.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: A useful lens for assessing conflict-risk premia: watch which specific actors gain from continuation (not the belligerents' stated goals) to forecast whether a war will actually end.
insights.quote: It is enough that it remains more advantageous than settlement for a few key actors capable of blocking a deal.
insights.locator: definition of managed instability

insights.claim: Kolbin builds on Thomas Schelling's 'The Diplomacy of Violence' (the power to hurt is bargaining power) and William Zartman's 'ripeness theory,' but inverts Zartman's framing: the danger in Ukraine and Iran is that key actors may conclude the war genuinely 'can go on like this' rather than reaching a ripe moment for peace.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: Signals that standard 'ripeness' indicators used by peace-process forecasters may not apply to these two conflicts; treat ceasefire talk as noise, not signal, until leverage-holding actors change their calculus.
insights.quote: the power to hurt [your enemy] is bargaining power
insights.locator: theoretical grounding section

insights.claim: A traditional military stalemate becomes 'managed instability' once actors build a political regime around exploiting the stalemate rather than the conflict simply freezing — tariffs, shipping, sanctions, energy, technology, supply chains, and outside support become the new instruments once decisive battlefield victory is off the table.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: Expect continued volatility in shipping insurance, energy transit chokepoints, and sanctions regimes as the primary theaters of ongoing escalation/de-escalation rather than front-line combat outcomes.
insights.locator: definition of managed instability

insights.claim: The Istanbul framework from spring 2022 is remembered as 'the road not taken' in Ukraine — after that point the conflict stopped resembling a quick war with a clear political endpoint and became a contest over leverage, import substitution, logistics corridors, and outside support.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: Reinforces that early-2022-style rapid diplomatic settlement windows in active wars are rare and, once missed, tend not to reopen for years.
insights.locator: The Original Ukraine Pattern

insights.claim: Since 2022, Russia has attacked along a roughly 1,200-kilometer front without achieving a decisive breakthrough, while Ukraine has been unable to retake all its territory by force — a mutual deadlock that pushed the conflict into grain, energy, ports, and 'shadow fleet' arenas as separate pressure points.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: Confirms the war's economic-warfare dimension (shadow fleet sanctions evasion, grain/energy infrastructure strikes) is a durable, investable theme independent of front-line movement.
insights.locator: The Original Ukraine Pattern

insights.claim: The Black Sea Grain Initiative operated for roughly a year as a narrow, practical arrangement that coexisted with continued war before Russia chose not to renew it, illustrating that such deals endure only as long as a party finds them useful.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: A precedent/base rate for how long narrow humanitarian or trade carve-outs (grain corridors, prisoner swaps, shipping arrangements) should be expected to last in either conflict — roughly a year — before being revoked as leverage.
insights.locator: discussion of the Black Sea Grain Initiative

insights.claim: Russia's continuation of the war lets it avoid admitting the failure of its original campaign, justifies tightened domestic control as wartime necessity, and buys time for its own military production and mobilization to catch up and for Western political change to shift in its favor.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: Explains why Moscow has structural incentives to wait out Western political cycles rather than negotiate now — relevant to timing bets on sanctions relief or a Ukraine settlement.
insights.locator: In Ukraine, managed instability serves the different interests

insights.claim: China gains access to a discounted Russian internal market and resources from prolonged war, the European Union sees continued Ukrainian resistance as containing Russia, and Central Asian states plus Gulf trade hubs have benefited from rerouted trade, new logistics corridors, and capital/business/skilled-worker inflows fleeing Russia.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: Identifies concrete third-party beneficiaries of continued war — discounted Russian commodities into China, capital/talent migration into Gulf and Central Asian hubs — as ongoing trade and FDI flows rather than one-off shocks.
insights.locator: Outside actors also have reasons to tolerate this conflict

themes.theme: Iran war compresses the Ukraine pattern

insights.claim: The Iran war is compressing years of the Ukrainian experience into months: overwhelming U.S. military pressure (including assassinations of top Iranian officials) failed to force a deal and instead pushed Tehran to make its Strait of Hormuz leverage central to the conflict.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: Frames Hormuz transit risk as a structural, recurring bargaining chip rather than a one-off crisis spike — relevant for tanker/insurance/energy-price risk premia over a multi-month-to-multi-year horizon.
insights.locator: When the Iran War Becomes Another Ukraine War

insights.claim: The Islamabad framework extended an earlier Iran ceasefire and created a 60-day negotiating window meant to reopen Hormuz and lift the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports, but pushed the hardest issues (nuclear question, sanctions, regional security) into a later phase that was never reached.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: Ceasefire announcements in the Iran conflict should be read as tactical pauses, not resolution — do not treat them as durable de-escalation signals for oil/shipping pricing.
insights.locator: The Islamabad framework extended an earlier ceasefire

insights.claim: By mid-June, Trump warned bombing could resume if he disliked the direction of negotiations, and it did resume along with Iranian strikes on Gulf states; after another two-week U.S. bombing campaign in late July, Washington again paused and Trump again cited 'good talks' while Tehran kept insisting it controlled Hormuz passage.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: Documents a repeating strikes-pause-talks-threats cycle in 2026 — a pattern to track for recurring volatility spikes in Gulf shipping and oil markets rather than expecting linear de-escalation.
insights.locator: By late July, after another two-week U.S. bombing campaign

insights.claim: The emerging Iran-Oman arrangement may restore Hormuz shipping (a U.S. goal) but would also institutionalize a larger Iranian coordinating role over Hormuz traffic, an outcome Washington has resisted, and its durability is uncertain — it could collapse the way the Black Sea Grain Initiative did once a party stops finding it useful.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: A specific, near-term catalyst to watch: an Iran-Oman shipping arrangement is a fragile, revocable fix for Hormuz risk, not a structural resolution — hedge accordingly rather than assuming it holds.
insights.locator: The emerging Iran-Oman arrangement

insights.claim: For Washington, continued Iran tension may normalize a permanent U.S. military role in Hormuz and sustained pressure on Tehran; for Tehran, it institutionalizes leverage over Hormuz, justifies tighter internal control, and deepens military-industrial cooperation with Russia and China.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: Suggests a durable U.S. force posture and cost base around Hormuz (relevant to defense/energy security budgets) alongside deepening Iran-Russia-China industrial ties (relevant to sanctions-evasion supply chains).
insights.locator: For Washington, it may normalize a permanent military role

insights.claim: Russia benefits from America's inability to simultaneously help both the Gulf and Ukraine, plus higher oil prices from the Iran conflict; China benefits from discounted Iranian oil and greater trade leverage over Tehran; Saudi Arabia and Oman benefit from reallocated regional infrastructure and investment as they try to distance themselves from the conflict zone.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: Higher-oil-price beneficiary set (Russia) and discounted-crude beneficiary set (China) are structurally opposed to a fast Iran settlement — a factor in why sanctions/diplomacy alone may not resolve the conflict quickly.
insights.locator: Russia benefits from America's inability

insights.claim: Iran has supported Russia's war in Ukraine since 2022, and in 2026 Russia is reportedly reciprocating by providing Iran military technology and targeting support, including for drone attacks on CIA facilities in the Gulf, while Ukraine exports its anti-drone expertise to Gulf states — creating a 'two-war proxy contest' where escalation in one theater changes the balance in the other.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: The Ukraine and Iran conflicts are no longer separable risk factors for portfolios — a shock in one (e.g., a major Hormuz incident) can be transmitted via technology/support flows into the other (e.g., Ukraine front-line dynamics), and vice versa.
insights.locator: From Parallel Wars to an Entangled Conflict System

insights.claim: Ukraine and the United Arab Emirates signed a 10-year defense cooperation agreement, with Kyiv stating the UAE would help Ukraine strengthen Black Sea security amid Russian attacks on Ukrainian shipping; Ukraine also reportedly received U.S. and French intelligence to conduct deep strikes inside Russia.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: A concrete new Gulf-Ukraine security link (10-year UAE pact) worth tracking for defense-industrial and Black Sea shipping-security implications.
insights.locator: Kyiv and Abu Dhabi have also signed a 10-year defense cooperation agreement

insights.claim: Both wars have depleted U.S. arms stocks and created competing demands for the same Western air-defense missile stockpile, since the drone-warfare technology and tactics developed in one theater transfer directly to the other while relying on shared Western defense production capacity.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: Direct read-through to sustained demand pressure on Western air-defense/missile manufacturers, with production capacity now contested between two simultaneous theaters rather than one.
insights.locator: both wars have depleted U.S. arms stocks

insights.claim: Because both proxy contests involve nuclear-armed initiators (the U.S./Russia dynamic), every failure to achieve original political objectives in either war adds pressure on leaders to seek new forms of escalation while claiming the escalation remains controllable — raising tail risk even though nuclear use itself is not the base case.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: A tail-risk factor for geopolitical hedging (volatility, gold, defense equities) that is structurally rising with each failed escalation cycle, not a static baseline risk.
insights.locator: The fact that two initiators are nuclear-armed states

insights.claim: A ceasefire in Ukraine would be a genuine positive (fewer deaths, calmer markets) but should not be read as the opposite of war — as the Iran case shows, a ceasefire is just one mechanism within a longer 'managed instability' confrontation, and a 'bad ceasefire' can simply prepare the next round of fighting.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: Contrarian risk-management point: don't fully unwind Ukraine-war hedges or geopolitical risk premia on ceasefire headlines alone — assess whether the underlying leverage structure actually changed.
insights.locator: A ceasefire in Ukraine (if observed) would obviously be a positive development

themes.theme: How to break the pattern (and why it's hard)

insights.claim: Kolbin identifies four conditions that together signal a war has entered 'managed instability': battlefield gains stop changing the actual power balance; ceasefires stop initiating an actual peace process; negotiations fragment into separate tracks (transit, sanctions, prisoners, energy, infrastructure); and the war expands geographically through outside allies, deep strikes, and alternative supply chains.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: A usable checklist for classifying any active conflict as having entered a durable, multi-year 'managed instability' regime versus still being on a path to resolution — useful for scenario-weighting geopolitical risk in portfolios.
insights.locator: Both Ukraine and Iran entered this form when four things happened together

insights.claim: Kolbin proposes reversing the sequence through which each war expanded — trading fewer attacks on ports/energy infrastructure for eased maritime restrictions, limits on targeting assistance for limits on deep strikes, and sanctions relief for monitored limits on rearmament — as coordinated steps toward, not substitutes for, a general settlement.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: Offers a template for reading future partial deals (port/shipping truces, targeting limits, sanctions-for-rearmament-limits swaps) as incremental de-escalation steps rather than full settlements — useful for calibrating market reaction to headline deals.
insights.locator: How to Break a 'Managed Instability' Logic

insights.claim: Early in the Trump administration, Washington paused military assistance and intelligence sharing to Ukraine to pressure Kyiv toward negotiations with Moscow, which helped secure Ukraine's acceptance of a U.S.-proposed 30-day ceasefire — but Russia did not accept the restraint, and Europe kept supporting Ukraine partly out of fear that an early settlement would let Moscow pose a greater danger later.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: A concrete precedent showing unilateral U.S. leverage (aid/intel pauses) can move Ukraine but not Russia — implying any durable settlement needs coordinated multilateral leverage (including on China) rather than U.S.-only pressure.
insights.locator: the United States has already tested this logic

insights.claim: Effective settlement conditioning would need to be coordinated and cooperative across Europe, Ukraine, the Gulf states, and China (using EU/U.S. market incentives to pressure Beijing on its Russia/Iran trade), combined with positive incentives like sanctions relief, restored trade, and security guarantees — not unilateral coercion alone.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: Implies any credible path to ending either war runs through joint Western leverage over China's trade with Russia/Iran — a factor to watch in EU/US trade and sanctions policy toward Beijing.
insights.locator: Effective settlement conditioning would therefore have to be coordinated
